The Morning Drip: mending fog nets, rain maps, and spoon mills

By Ada Rivers
October 27, 2026

This is the made-up edition of The Morning Drip, a daily newsletter about water and the people who move it around.

The people who mend the fog nets

Every autumn a small crew walks the ridge above the village with needles, spare mesh and a flask of tea. They check each net by hand, one square at a time, looking for the tears the summer wind has made.

The work is slow and quiet. A single torn square can halve what a net collects, so the crew mends even the small ones, tying each knot twice so that the next storm does not undo it before spring.

Most of the menders learned the job from a parent or a neighbour. There is no school for it and no manual, only the habit of looking closely and the patience to keep going after the light has gone flat.

The village pays them in water. Each mender's household gets the first share of what the nets collect in the dry months, which in a bad year is the only reason the gardens survive until the rains come back.

Younger people are taking the work up again, the crew says, now that the nets are known beyond the valley. Two of them started this year, and both say the view from the ridge at dawn is most of the pay.

One more thing

A rain map drawn by a schoolteacher a century ago turns out to match the modern records almost line for line. She walked every path in the valley with a jar and a notebook, and kept at it for eleven years.

Find out how the old map was found.

—Bo Lindqvist

Small pleasures

A place for small and cheerful things to brighten up the day. (Got one? Write to me.)

+ Watch a whole valley fill with morning fog in this calm time-lapse.
+ A cat has learned to open the garden gate, and the neighbours are filming it.
+ Someone has built a tiny working water mill out of old spoons.
+ These are the oddest weather records ever set, from hail to heat.
